analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects servicemembers from mortgage foreclosure for nine months after they return from military service.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: introduced in February 2011, it sat in the House Veterans' Affairs subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: When a servicemember has a mortgage and is deployed, current law stops lenders from foreclosing during military service and for a short window afterward. Congress had temporarily stretched that window from 90 days to 9 months, but it was scheduled to shrink back to 90 days in 2011. This bill would make the 9-month protection permanent, giving troops time after deployment to sort out their finances before losing a home.
analysis.who_benefits: Military homeowners on active duty. Under the temporary version of the law, a servicemember had nine months after leaving duty status before a lender could foreclose on a pre-service mortgage. The bill would have locked that in permanently instead of letting it lapse back to 90 days, protecting deployed troops and their families from losing homes over missed payments caused by deployment.

how_it_helps.text: Changes the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act so the foreclosure-protection window after military service is 9 months instead of 90 days, permanently [S3].
Extends the same 9-month window to a servicemember's right to pause court proceedings over a pre-service property obligation [S3].
The temporary 9-month period had already lapsed back to 90 days on January 1, 2011, so the bill would have restored the longer protection [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and the investors who hold the loans, who would have to wait nine months after service ends before foreclosing on a pre-service mortgage, delaying their ability to take back and resell the property.

drawbacks.text: The protection applies only to loans taken out before military service, so it cannot be used as a broad shield, and lenders retain the right to foreclose once the window closes [S3].

A longer, permanent foreclosure delay raises carrying costs for lenders and loan investors, which critics could argue gets priced into the cost or availability of mortgages for borrowers, including servicemembers themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: a family whose breadwinner is deployed does not lose a home to a technical default in the months right after service ends. The cost falls on lenders, and any spillover into mortgage pricing is speculative and modest compared with the harm foreclosures do to military families. This is a narrow, well-designed protection, not an overreach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and then to its Economic Opportunity subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bob Filner introduced the bill on February 8, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs the same day [S5].
In March 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and no further action was recorded through the end of the 112th Congress [S5].
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, 6 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
Under the law in effect at the time, the 9-month foreclosure-protection period had already reverted to 90 days on January 1, 2011 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers kept the shorter 90-day protection window, which had lapsed back from 9 months in 2011, meaning deployed troops' families faced foreclosure sooner. Military homeowners gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Bob Filner
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), sponsor and chair of the House Veterans' Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently extend the 9-month foreclosure protection and referred it through committee channels.

for.name: 6 House Democrats and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

against.name: House Committee on Veterans' Affairs / Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing or markup, letting it die in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 6 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsors, with no recorded opposition and no votes taken.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to wait nine months after military service ends before foreclosing on a pre-service mortgage, delaying recoveries on loans. The bill's death preserved the shorter 90-day window. Because nothing advanced, the industry's interest in the outcome ran against the families the bill was written to protect.
